summary: A country in western central Africa on the west bank of the Congo River, formerly part of French Equatorial Africa, independent in 1960, with oil as its main export.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was first introduced at the end of the 15th century when the Portuguese made contact with the Kingdom of Kongo, but it took real root in what is now the Republic of the Congo only after the 1880s, when the French explorer Brazza established the colony of French Congo and in 1883 Spiritan missionaries set up a mission station at Loango. In the colonial period the Catholic Church controlled most of education and trained political elites, including the first president, Fulbert Youlou, who was himself a Catholic priest.

ranking.name: Protestantism and independent churches
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced in 1909 by the Swedish Mission Covenant Church, which established churches and schools in the Pool region of the south and among the Kongo people and later developed into the Evangelical Church of the Congo. Swedish missionaries preached in Kikongo and translated the Bible, giving Protestantism a deep foundation among the Kongo of the south; in recent years various independent churches have also grown rapidly in the cities.

ranking.name: Awakening (revival) churches and other Christians
ranking.description: The revival churches are Pentecostal and charismatic churches that have grown rapidly since the 1990s; during and after the 1993–1999 civil wars in the Congo, many people turned to new churches emphasizing miracles, healing and prosperity theology. These churches are especially active in cities such as Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire and have attracted large numbers of young followers.

ranking.name: Indigenous-Christian syncretic movements (such as the Kimbanguist Church)
ranking.description: These movements blend Christianity with indigenous beliefs and include the Kimbanguist Church originating in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the 'Matsouanism' movement begun in the Congo by André Matswa in the 1920s, the latter known for its anti-colonial struggle; after Matswa died in prison in 1942 his followers regarded him as a messiah. These churches reflect the self-directed religious and political awakening of Africans during the colonial period.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced in the colonial period by West African merchants, and today most Muslims are merchants from Mali, Senegal, Mauritania and other West African countries and their descendants, concentrated in the commercial districts of Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire. Because it arrived late and mostly through foreign merchants, Muslims make up only about 2%.

religion.background: Before colonization the Republic of the Congo was the site of states such as the Kingdom of Kongo, the Kingdom of Loango and the Kingdom of Tio, and religion was mainly ancestor and nature belief. After French colonization in the 1880s, Catholic and Protestant missionaries entered one after another, and the colonial period also saw indigenous denominations such as the Matsouanist movement that blended Christianity with anti-colonial thought. After independence in 1960, the People's Republic of the Congo practiced Marxism-Leninism from 1969 to 1991, and religion was subject to certain restrictions. After democratization and the civil wars of the 1990s, revival churches and various new denominations grew rapidly.

ranking.name: Kongo (Kituba)
ranking.description: Kituba, the lingua franca form of Kongo, is a simplified common language based on Kikongo that developed from the late 19th century into the colonial period among river traders and laborers from various places; the gathering of large numbers of workers during the building of the Congo-Ocean Railway in 1921–1934 spread it further along the railway. Today it is the main lingua franca of the south, Pointe-Noire and southern Brazzaville, and is one of the two national languages of the Republic of the Congo.

ranking.name: Lingala
ranking.description: Lingala originates from the Bangala language of the middle Congo River and spread with river trade and colonial armies from the late 19th century, becoming the lingua franca along the Congo River. The capital Brazzaville and Kinshasa on the opposite bank face each other across the river, and the popular music of both (such as rumba) is sung in Lingala, which has made it widely popular in the north and the capital; it is one of the two national languages.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French arrived with French colonization in the 1880s, and Brazzaville was the capital of 'Free France' during the Second World War in 1940–1943. After independence in 1960 French remained the sole official language, used in government, education and the media, but because Kituba and Lingala are mostly used in daily life, only about 5% have French as their mother tongue.

language.history: The Republic of the Congo has about 60 languages, mostly of the Bantu family, including Kongo in the south, Mbochi in the north and Teke in the center. After the late 19th century, Lingala spread with trade on the Congo River, and railway building in the colonial period made Kituba the lingua franca of the south. After French colonization in the 1880s, French became the language of administration and education, and it became the official language after independence in 1960. Today the Republic of the Congo shows a pattern of Kituba spoken in the south, Lingala in the north, and French as the official language of the whole country.

ranking.name: Chikwangue (cassava bread)
ranking.description: Cassava is soaked in water to ferment and pounded into a paste, wrapped in banana or bamboo leaves into long sticks and steamed, with a firm, elastic texture and a slight sourness.
ranking.history: Cassava is native to South America and was brought by the Portuguese to the coast of the Kingdom of Kongo in the 16th century and then inland along the Congo River, becoming a staple because it is drought-tolerant and high-yielding. Fermenting and wrapping before steaming removes the cyanide from cassava and lets chikwangue keep for days to weeks, suited to long journeys and river voyages. Today chikwangue can be seen everywhere in the markets of Brazzaville, often eaten with grilled fish.

ranking.name: Foufou
ranking.description: Cassava flour is stirred with hot water into an elastic dough-like staple, with a sticky, slippery texture and mild flavor, pinched into small balls by hand and dipped in stews or sauces.
ranking.history: Foufou is a staple shared by the Congo basin and West Africa, spelled 'foufou' in French. Cassava became more widespread in the colonial period because the French authorities promoted its planting to prevent famine. In the Republic of the Congo foufou appears at almost every meal, served with dishes such as cassava leaf stew and palm-oil chicken, the foundation of the family diet.

ranking.name: Saka-saka / Pondu (cassava leaf stew)
ranking.description: A green stew in which cassava leaves are pounded and stewed for a long time with palm oil, peanut butter, onion, and dried or smoked fish, with a thick texture.
ranking.history: Cassava leaf stew is called 'saka-saka' in the Republic of the Congo and 'pondu' in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, reflecting the food culture shared on both banks of the Congo River. Cassava leaves are rich in protein and vitamins and are an important source of nutrition for many families. In the Republic of the Congo this dish often appears at weekend family meals and festivals, served with chikwangue or rice.

ranking.name: Poulet à la moambé (palm nut chicken)
ranking.description: Chicken is stewed in a thick sauce made by cooking palm fruit, with onion, garlic and chili, orange-red in color and with a rich sauce, often served with rice.
ranking.history: Palm nut chicken is a traditional dish shared across central Africa, and 'moambé' is the name for palm sauce in the Congo basin. The oil palm is a plant native to the tropical rainforest of central Africa, and for thousands of years local people have made cooking oil and sauces from palm fruit. In the Republic of the Congo this dish often appears at festivals and when entertaining guests, a famous home dish that shows sincerity.

ranking.name: Poisson braisé (grilled fish)
ranking.description: A whole fish is marinated with spices, garlic and chili and grilled over charcoal, eaten with fried plantain, chikwangue and a chili-onion sauce, charred outside and tender inside.
ranking.history: The Congo River and the Atlantic coast are rich in fish, and grilled fish is one of the most common dishes in the Republic of the Congo. At night the open-air bars and restaurants along the Congo River in Brazzaville often have grilled-fish stalls, where people listen to Lingala rumba music while eating grilled fish, an important part of the local nightlife. Pointe-Noire is known for its Atlantic sea fish, and grilled fish is often enjoyed with local beer.
